source.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
source.authors: Leonard Bereska; Zoe Tzifa-Kratira; Reza Samavi; E. Gavves

record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature compression/superposition using SAE activation entropy, a different method from the original toy-model weight-based analysis, and reports results on toy networks, Pythia-70M, and other settings.
record.gate_note: The toy-model correlation result validates the measurement pipeline, but does not itself report the sparsity-dependent geometric transition. Results on algorithmic tasks and adversarial training measure effective feature counts and compression; they do not directly measure neuron-level polysemanticity or feature directions. Cited results from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds an SAE-activation entropy measure of effective features. It applies the measure to Pythia-70M, finding effective features far above neuron count (V4). It also tests whether SAE-derived counts converge as dictionary size grows, under different ℓ1 settings (V5). Most other results are capacity or adversarial-training effects on its own metric and fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Additions: the authors present the entropy measure as validated in toy models (r = 0.94) and say it should be read comparatively, not as absolute counts. They say adversarial training splits into abundance and scarcity regimes, contradicting the hypothesis that it universally reduces superposition. They call the application findings preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE activation entropy as its main measure rather than the original toy-model weight-based geometry measure. It includes a toy-model validation, but its broader analyses concern dropout, algorithmic tasks, Pythia-70M, and adversarial training.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature counts depend on SAE dictionary size and ℓ1 regularization; weak regularization permits feature splitting and excessive regularization suppresses features. Adversarial-training effects also vary with task complexity, dataset difficulty, network capacity, and layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout lowers effective features by up to 50%, although dropout is reported elsewhere to raise polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise-induced redundancy can raise polysemanticity while lowering superposition, so the two dissociate.

fits_no_version.finding: Compressed Tracr models reach F ≈ N and then lose performance, never reaching ψ > 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Without sparse inputs, compression does not produce superposition beyond the lossless limit.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial training raises or lowers effective features depending on task complexity and capacity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of adversarial training on superposition depends on the ratio of task demands to capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective features consolidate sharply at the grokking transition and correlate with LLC (r = 0.908).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition measures track developmental phase transitions.

fits_no_version.finding: The SAE entropy measure correlates r = 0.94 with a weight-based reference in toy models.

record.problems: The paper describes its application findings as preliminary and exploratory. The measurement depends on SAE quality, regularization, dictionary size, and activation distribution. The authors note feature splitting, ghost features, incomplete coverage, feature correlations, and limitations of the linear-feature and independence assumptions. Some adversarial-training patterns remain unexplained; the text reports weaker significance for equivalent MLP experiments than CNN experiments.

untested.parts: The sparsity-dependent transition and the nearly orthogonal geometry are not reported as the study's own results. The toy models serve only to validate the metric.
Neuron polysemanticity, and dedicated dimensions for important features, are not measured.
Polysemantic neurons are not measured. The dropout argument is interpretive only.
Only Pythia-70M with pretrained SAEs is tested. Spreading of features across neurons is not measured, and larger LLMs are not tested.
Not tested: whether SAE features are the same units across seeds or SAEs, whether they are complete, and whether they are canonical. Only effective-count convergence on sparse parity is tested.
1-D versus multi-dimensional features are not compared. The linear assumption is listed as a limitation.

missing.what: Layer-wise effective feature counts across Pythia-70M components. MLPs are highest and attention minimal, with a non-monotonic 'hunchback' across layers. Whether attention layers exceed N is unclear.
Reference ψ in toy models ranges about 1–4 across the sparsity sweep, an implicit sparsity dependence that is not stated numerically.
Toy-model correlation degrades at extreme ℓ1, small dictionaries and very large dictionaries.

record.verdict_notes: This paper is mainly a measurement-method contribution. V4 support depends entirely on pretrained SAEs and on the paper's own metric. The 5,600 versus 10,000 discrepancy for Pythia MLP1 should be resolved before citing a ψ value. The authors argue (Sec. 2, 6.1) that polysemanticity can arise without superposition, which is relevant to V3 but unmeasured here.

versions.untested_parts: The paper discusses the toy-model account and tests whether its SAE metric tracks a toy-model reference, but does not report its own result testing the sparsity-dependent transition or the nearly orthogonal geometry.

The study reports capacity-dependent changes in effective feature counts, but does not measure neuron-level polysemanticity, dedicated dimensions for important features, or feature sharing by importance.
It distinguishes polysemanticity from superposition in its discussion, but does not measure polysemantic neurons or test their occurrence independently of superposition.
The LLM analysis is limited to Pythia-70M and uses pretrained SAEs; it does not establish that this pattern generalizes to LLMs broadly or independently validate the SAE feature recovery.

The study tests feature-count convergence as dictionary size changes under different regularization strengths, but does not establish SAE features as complete, stable, canonical units across models or training procedures.
The SAE is designed to represent features as directions, but the study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional feature geometry.

rows.subject: toy models (aggregate of 100 models)
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE-activation entropy estimates with the toy-model weight-based reference across a sparsity sweep.
rows.measure: Correlation between SAE-activation entropy superposition measure and reference values from toy-model weights
rows.note: This validates agreement between measurement methods; it does not report the toy models’ sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
rows.check: This is the study's own method validated against a weight-based reference, not a result on toy-model geometry. Keep as none.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Measured entropy-based effective feature counts from pretrained SAE activations.
rows.measure: Effective features; compared with number of SAE features activating
rows.note: The text reports an effective feature count and a 20×-neurons compression figure for MLP 1.
rows.check: Baseline should be the 512-dim layer width, not '21,000 SAE features activate'. Values disagree in the text: it gives 5,600 effective features (~11× of 512), but the Fig. 6a caption says MLP1 peaks at 10,000 features (20× neurons). Record both and flag the inconsistency.

rows.subject: multi-task sparse parity networks (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Swept SAE dictionary expansion and ℓ1 regularization, measuring feature-count convergence.
rows.measure: Effective feature count as dictionary size increases
rows.value: Feature counts plateau despite dictionary expansion
rows.note: The plateau supports convergence under the stated regularization, but does not establish canonical feature identity.
rows.check: Only the effective count plateaus with ℓ1 ≥ 0.1. Feature identity, completeness and cross-seed stability are not measured.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5: effective-count convergence does not establish complete, stable, canonical feature identities.
source_check.problem: The partial state treats untested feature identity and completeness as an observed incomplete effect.

rows.subject: multi-task sparse parity networks (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature counts while increasing SAE dictionary size with weak regularization.
rows.measure: Feature-count growth as dictionary size increases
rows.value: Continued growth across all tested scales; attributed to feature splitting
rows.note: The study says the growth reflects SAE decomposition of computational features into spurious finer components, rather than genuine superposition.
rows.check: No convergence with ℓ1 = 0.01. The authors attribute the continued growth to SAE feature splitting.

rows.subject: multi-task sparse parity networks (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature counts while increasing SAE dictionary size with excessive regularization.
rows.note: The paper reports that excessive regularization suppresses features.
rows.check: Features are suppressed with ℓ1 = 10. No numbers are given.

rows.subject: MLPs on multi-task sparse parity (aggregate over h ∈ {16, 32, 64, 128})
rows.operation_detail: Applied dropout to hidden activations and measured effective features.

conditions.value: multi-task sparse parity, 3 tasks, 4 bits each

rows.note: The authors interpret the reduction as dropout-related redundant encoding consuming capacity and less essential features being pruned.
rows.check: Polysemanticity is not measured. The contrast with Marshall & Kirchner's dropout-polysemanticity result is argued, not measured, so the row cannot be linked to V3.

rows.subject: Tracr sequence-reversal models (compiled and trained from scratch, aggregate)
rows.size_stated: compiled model originally 45D; compressed dimensions varied
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective features while compressing residual-stream activations.

conditions.value: compiled models and transformers trained from scratch

rows.measure: Effective feature count and superposition ratio
rows.value: Converged to 12 features; ψ ≈ 0.3 initially and approaches ψ = 1, with further compression reducing features and eventually collapsing performance
rows.note: The study says these algorithmic tasks do not exhibit ψ > 1; it attributes this to lack of sparse activation patterns.

rows.subject: Tracr sequence-sorting models (compiled and trained from scratch, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective features while compressing residual-stream activations.

conditions.value: compiled models and transformers trained from scratch

rows.measure: Effective feature count and superposition ratio
rows.value: Converged to 10 features; F ≈ N during compression, with further compression reducing features and eventually collapsing performance
rows.note: The study reports resistance to ψ > 1 and attributes it to the tasks’ lack of sparse activation patterns.

rows.subject: two-path MLP on modular arithmetic
rows.size_stated: embedding dimension 12; hidden dimension 48; 53 output classes
rows.operation_detail: Tracked feature count during grokking and compared it with the Local Learning Coefficient.
rows.measure: Feature-count dynamics and correlation with LLC
rows.baseline: LLC shows initial proliferation followed by smooth decay
rows.value: Feature count shows sharp consolidation at the generalization transition; r = 0.908, p < 0.001 with LLC
rows.note: This developmental result is not directly covered by the listed claim versions.

rows.subject: MLPs and CNNs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized feature-count slopes as adversarial-training strength increased.
rows.measure: Effective feature-count change relative to ϵ = 0 baseline
rows.value: Positive slopes; feature counts expand up to 2× baseline
rows.note: The authors report that binary classification consistently produces positive slopes.

rows.subject: MLPs and CNNs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized feature-count slopes as adversarial-training strength increased.
rows.measure: Effective feature-count change relative to ϵ = 0 baseline
rows.value: Feature counts decrease by up to 60%, particularly in early layers
rows.note: This is an outcome for the measured feature-count proxy, not a direct measurement of feature geometry.

rows.subject: MLPs and CNNs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature-count response across adversarial-training strengths.
rows.measure: Effective feature-count change relative to baseline
rows.value: Inverted-U pattern: moderate training initially expands features, stronger training triggers reduction
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative pattern but no separate numerical values for this condition.

rows.subject: MNIST and Fashion-MNIST models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized adversarial-training feature-count slopes by dataset difficulty.
rows.note: Fashion-MNIST produced systematically more negative slopes than MNIST.

rows.subject: single-layer MLPs and CNNs on MNIST (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized feature-count slopes across network capacities.

conditions.value: narrow networks: 8–32 units; wide networks: 128–512 units

rows.measure: Meta-analytic feature-count slope per adversarial-training strength
rows.value: Meta-analytic slope = 0.220 ± 0.037, z = 5.90, p < 0.001; minimal-capacity networks show negative slopes, while high-capacity networks show positive slopes
rows.note: The paper reports the capacity-dependent direction change and states that the lowest-capacity networks reduce features across task complexities.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized feature-count slopes against network width.
rows.value: 31.0 ± 2.0 per log(width), t(2) = 15.7, p = 0.004, R² = 0.929; an 8-fold width increase produces a 65-unit normalized-slope change
rows.note: The text says slopes approach 80 at double width and that feature expansion rises strongly with width.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer-wise effective feature-count changes under adversarial training.

conditions.value: conv1, layer1, middle layers, layer3, layer4

rows.measure: Layer-wise feature-count ratio relative to baseline
rows.value: Early layers reduce features by up to 50%; middle layers remain stable; deep layers expand up to 4×; narrowing to 1/4 width removes late-layer expansion while early reduction persists but weakens
rows.note: The authors say the layer-wise pattern is dampened as width decreases.

relationships.condition: Pythia-70M, MLP 1 output, pretrained Marks et al. SAEs
relationships.reason: The entropy measure gives 5,600 (text) or 10,000 (caption) effective features in a 512-dim layer, well beyond the neuron count (r2). The two figures are inconsistent.
relationships.display_finding: The entropy measure gave 5,600 (in the text) or 10,000 (in a caption) effective features in a 512-dimensional layer, well beyond the neuron count. The two figures disagree.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Pythia-70M, MLP 1 output, pretrained Marks et al. SAEs
source_check.reason: Section 6.4 reports 5,600 effective features; Figure 6a's caption reports 10,000. Both exceed the 512-dimensional layer and support V4's indirect evidence, subject to the metric's proxy interpretation.

relationships.reason: Effective counts plateau with dictionary size, but only the count stabilises; feature identity is untested (r3).
relationships.display_finding: The effective number of features plateaued as dictionary size grew, but only that number stabilised; whether the same features were learned was not tested.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r3 measures convergence of effective counts, not feature identity, completeness or canonicality. Untested properties cannot justify limits_scope.

relationships.reason: Counts grow without bound (splitting) or collapse, depending on ℓ1 (r4, r5). The authors state absolute counts depend on SAE configuration.
relationships.display_finding: At ℓ1 = 0.01 the effective number grew without bound through splitting, and at 10 it collapsed; the authors state absolute values depend on SAE configuration.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r4 and r5 show extraction depends on regularization: weak regularization produces spurious feature splitting, while excessive regularization suppresses features entirely. These results qualify an unconditional canonical-inventory interpretation.
